title: Advanced
summary: Pawn structure, key endgames and planning.

steps.text: A pawn with no friendly pawns on the files beside it is isolated. No pawn can ever protect it.

steps.prompt: Tap White’s isolated pawn.
steps.explanation: No white pawn stands on the c- or e-file.

steps.prompt: Where does the other side like to put a piece against an isolated pawn?
options: On the square in front of it
steps.explanation: No pawn can chase a piece away from there.

steps.text: An isolated pawn has a plus side too: open files beside it for your rooks, and room for your pieces.
Two pawns of one side on the same file are doubled. They cannot protect each other.

steps.prompt: Tap both doubled pawns.
steps.explanation: Both sit on the c-file.

steps.text: A backward pawn has fallen behind its neighbours and cannot safely move forward.

steps.prompt: Is a doubled pawn always bad?
options: No, it can open a file and guard squares
steps.explanation: Weigh its downsides against what it gives you.

steps.text: Pawns on a diagonal, each protecting the next, form a chain.

steps.prompt: Where is a pawn chain weakest?
steps.explanation: The base has no pawn protecting it.

steps.text: Attack the base of your opponent’s chain, and play on the side of the board where your chain points.
Having more pawns than your opponent on one side of the board is a majority. Push it to make a passed pawn.

steps.prompt: Tap White’s passed pawn.
steps.explanation: No black pawn can stop it on the a-, b- or c-file.

steps.prompt: Which majority makes a passed pawn far from the kings?
options: A queenside majority after castling short
A kingside majority after castling short
steps.explanation: The kings are on the kingside, so a passed pawn on the other side is hard to stop.

steps.text: Two pawns can attack three: pushing them creates a weak pawn in the larger group.

steps.prompt: In this structure, which pawns does White push in a minority attack?
steps.explanation: White has two queenside pawns against Black’s three.

steps.text: After b5 and bxc6, Black is left with a weak pawn to defend for the rest of the game.
Rooks belong behind passed pawns: yours to push them, the other side’s to stop them.

steps.prompt: Put your rook behind the passed pawn.
steps.hint: The pawn is on the a-file.
steps.explanation: The rook gets stronger with every step the pawn takes.

steps.prompt: Win the rook endgame.

steps.text: A rook on a file or rank can fence the enemy king out, so your king and pawn walk forward freely.

steps.prompt: Your rook cuts the black king off along a file. What does that do?
options: Keeps the king away from your pawn
steps.explanation: The king cannot cross the rook’s file.

steps.prompt: Use your rook well.

steps.text: With king and pawn on the seventh against a rook, first fence the enemy king out with your rook.

steps.prompt: The black king is cut off. Build the bridge: rook to the fourth rank.
steps.explanation: When your king steps out, the rook on e4 will block the checks.

steps.text: Your king then walks out, and when the checks come, your rook steps in to block them.
Defending rook and pawn with a rook, keep your rook on your third rank so the enemy king cannot advance.

steps.prompt: Black to move. Put your rook on the sixth rank to stop the king.
steps.hint: The sixth rank is your third rank.
steps.explanation: The white king cannot step onto the sixth rank.

steps.text: When the pawn advances to the sixth, swing your rook to the back and check from behind.
In rook endgames an active rook is often worth a pawn. Attack, do not just defend.

steps.prompt: Your rook can guard a pawn passively or attack the enemy pawns. Usually you should…
steps.explanation: An active rook keeps the other side busy.

steps.prompt: Keep your rook active.

steps.text: Bishops like open boards and pawns on both sides. Knights like closed positions and pawns on one side.

steps.prompt: Pawns on both wings, open lines. Which piece do you want?
steps.explanation: A bishop crosses the board in one move.

steps.prompt: Use the minor piece.

steps.text: King, bishop and rook pawn against a lone king is usually a draw if the bishop cannot cover the corner.

steps.prompt: White has an h-pawn and a light-squared bishop. h8 is dark. If the black king reaches h8…
steps.explanation: The bishop can never drive the king out of a dark corner.

steps.text: When ahead, check the promotion square’s colour before trading into such an ending.
A queen beats a pawn on the seventh by checking until the king blocks its pawn, then bringing her king closer.

steps.prompt: Stop the pawn: check and pin until the black king blocks it.
steps.explanation: The king stands in front of the pawn, so your king gains a move each time.

steps.prompt: What does each check aim for?
options: To force the king in front of its pawn
To take the pawn at once
steps.explanation: With the king on the promotion square, your own king can step closer.

steps.text: If each side has one bishop and they run on different colours, endings are often drawn even a pawn or two down.

steps.prompt: You are a pawn behind with opposite-coloured bishops. What should you try?
steps.explanation: The defender’s bishop can blockade on squares the other bishop never reaches.

steps.text: In the middlegame the same bishops favour the attacker, since neither bishop can defend the other’s squares.
Bring pieces toward the enemy king before you strike. Three attackers against two defenders usually win.

steps.prompt: Before attacking the king, what should you count?
options: The pawns on the other side
steps.explanation: Attack where you have more pieces.

steps.prompt: Break through.

steps.text: When kings castle on opposite sides, both players push pawns at the other king. Speed matters most.

steps.prompt: Kings castled on opposite sides. What should you do?
steps.explanation: The faster attack usually wins.

steps.prompt: Attack on the queenside.

steps.text: Giving up material is worth it when it opens the king, for example a bishop taken on h7 with check.

steps.prompt: When is a sacrifice worth it?
options: When you can follow up with more threats
steps.explanation: Calculate the follow-up before you give anything away.

steps.prompt: Find the sacrifice.

steps.text: Under attack, find the one move that stops the threat. Trading attackers is often the best defence.

steps.prompt: Your opponent attacks with many pieces. Which trade helps most?
steps.explanation: Fewer attackers means less danger.

steps.prompt: Find the defence.

steps.text: List a few candidate moves before you choose: checks, captures, threats, then quiet improving moves.

steps.prompt: Why list several moves before choosing?
options: So you do not miss a better one
steps.explanation: The first move you see is not always best.

steps.prompt: Find the best move.

steps.text: After each move by your opponent, ask: what do they want to do next? Then decide whether to stop it.

steps.prompt: Your opponent wants to play a knight to a strong square. What can you do?
steps.explanation: Taking away a good square is often the best move.

steps.prompt: Stop the threat.

lessons.title: Turning an advantage into a win

steps.text: When ahead, keep it simple: remove your opponent’s chances, trade pieces and push your extra pawn.

steps.prompt: You are a piece up. What is the safest plan?
steps.explanation: Simple play keeps the advantage.

steps.prompt: Finish the job.

steps.text: Picture the board after each move in a line. Start with forcing moves, which leave the fewest replies.

steps.prompt: Which lines are easiest to see far ahead?
steps.explanation: Forcing moves limit the other side’s choices.

steps.prompt: See the mate coming.
